title: What If You Could See How Much People Trust You?
hook: I woke up seeing numbers above every head
description:
One morning Leo wakes up and sees a number above every head: how much that person trusts him. His mom is at 64%, a quiet kid he barely knows is at 92%, and his best friend since kindergarten is at 31% and falling. An original animated story about small promises, big mistakes and earning trust back.

#whatif #story #animation

scenes.say: You said seven, Leo. You swore. I looked at that door the whole night.
I know. I'm sorry. Practice ran late, and then my phone died, and...
Your phone always dies. It's the most tired phone in the world.
She hung up. It was her first art show. Six paintings, one tiny gallery, and one empty chair she'd saved for me.
I told myself it didn't matter. She always forgave me. Then I went to sleep, and the next morning, everything changed.
Mom was making toast. And floating above her head, in bright orange, was a number. Sixty-four percent.
Why are you staring at my hair? Is something in it?
I rubbed my eyes. The number stayed. It even wobbled when she moved, like a balloon tied to her head.
Outside, the bus driver had one. Fifty. The lady with the dog, fifty. Every stranger on the street, fifty percent.
First period, I tested theories. Grades? No. Mr. Hale, our teacher, had seventy-one, and I'm failing his class.
Was it how much people liked me? No. Jordan, the loudest guy in school, gave me a high five. His number said twenty-eight.
Everybody likes Jordan. Jordan likes everyone. But twenty-eight looked like a warning label.
Then I saw Maya at her locker. And above her head, in angry red, was a number I'll never forget.
Thirty-one percent.
Thirty-one. My best friend since kindergarten. The girl who once gave me her chickenpox on purpose, so we could stay home together.
Don't. I'm not mad. I'm just tired, Leo.
Her number didn't move. It just sat there, red, like a bill I hadn't paid.
That night at dinner, Mom asked about my history test. The one I'd told her I crushed.
I didn't crush it. I got a fifty-two, folded into a very small square in my backpack.
So? How did it go? You said you studied all weekend.
I opened my mouth to lie. And I watched her number. Then, as the lie formed, I panicked and said the truth instead.
I got a fifty-two, Mom. I didn't study. I played games all weekend and lied about it.
She put her fork down. I waited for the yelling. Instead, the number above her head clicked up. Sixty-five. Sixty-six.
That's when I got it. These numbers weren't love, or popularity. They showed how much each person trusted me.
Strangers start at fifty. A coin flip. Everyone else had been adjusting their number for years, one promise at a time.
Thank you for telling me. I'm still disappointed. But thank you.
Lies are expensive, Leo. You just never see the bill.
That night I made a list. Every person in my life, and their number. Mom, sixty-six. Mr. Hale, seventy-one. Coach, forty.
Maya, thirty-one. I kept staring at that one. How do you get that low with someone who's known you for eleven years?
So I went through it. The art show. Her birthday, when I showed up two hours late with a gas station card.
The time I promised to help move her grandma's piano, and forgot. The summer I said I'd write every week, and wrote once.
None of them felt big. Each one, alone, was just a small sorry. But stacked together, they built a wall.
I always thought trust was like a light switch. On or off. It's not. It's a jar, filling or leaking one drop at a time.
And mine had been leaking for years.
The next morning, something strange happened. A kid named Theo walked past me in the hall.
Theo is quiet. He eats lunch alone, reads thick books, and wears the same green hoodie every day. I barely knew him.
And above his head, glowing bright green, was ninety-two percent.
Ninety-two. Higher than my mom. Higher than anyone. From a kid I'd said maybe ten words to in my whole life.
Hey, uh, Theo. Weird question. Why do you... trust me?
That is a weird question. You really don't remember fifth grade?
I didn't. So he told me. In fifth grade, his parents were splitting up. He cried in the boys' bathroom every day at lunch.
One day, I walked in and saw him. I said, I won't tell anyone. Then I gave him half my sandwich and left.
You never told anyone. Not once. Anyone else would have. You didn't.
I'd forgotten the whole thing. One promise. Kept almost by accident. And he'd carried it for six years.
So that was the other side of it. Broken promises add up. But so do kept ones. And kept ones last longer.
Also, you returned my calculator in seventh grade. With new batteries. That was a power move.
I laughed for the first time in two days. And for the first time, I had a plan.
If promises build trust, I'd just make a lot of promises. And keep them all. How hard could it be?
Monday. I promised Mr. Hale I'd retake the test on Thursday. His number went up to seventy-four.
I promised Coach I'd come early to every practice. Forty-three. I promised Mom I'd do the dishes every night. Sixty-eight.
I promised Theo I'd sit with him at lunch on Wednesday. He looked at me like I'd handed him a puppy. Ninety-three.
And I promised Maya I'd help with her portfolio. The big one. Her application to the art academy in the city.
Saturday, nine in the morning. The canvases are huge, I can't carry them alone on the bus. Don't promise if you won't come.
I'll be there. Eight thirty. I swear. Her number twitched. Thirty-one. Thirty-two. She didn't believe me. Not yet.
By Tuesday night, I'd made nineteen promises. I wrote them on my hand, then my arm, then a sticky note on my forehead.
Wednesday came. Lunch. Theo was waiting at his usual table, alone, with two milk cartons. One for me.
Then Jordan yelled across the cafeteria. Leo! We saved you a seat! The popular table. The one I'd wanted since freshman year.
I froze between two tables. One full of people who barely knew me. One with a kid who'd trusted me for six years.
I'm not proud of it. I went to Jordan's table. Just for a minute, I told myself. Just to say hi.
I stayed the whole lunch. When I looked back, Theo's milk carton was still sitting there. Unopened.
And his number. Ninety-three. Ninety. Eighty-five. Eighty. Still green. But falling. Like it was finally learning something about me.
And something else happened at that table. Something that would ruin my whole week.
Jordan leaned in. So, is it true Maya's leaving? Art school in the city? I shrugged. And then I opened my mouth.
She hasn't even applied yet. Don't tell anyone, it's a secret. Jordan smiled. His number didn't move. Twenty-eight.
By sixth period, the whole school knew. Maya's leaving. Maya thinks she's too good for us. Maya's ditching her friends.
I found her by the art room. Her eyes were red. And her number... I'd never seen a number that low on someone I knew.
Four percent.
I told one person, Leo. One. You.
I didn't tell the whole school! I told Jordan, and only because he already guessed...
So you did tell.
I could explain all day. It wouldn't matter. She wasn't judging one moment. She was judging eleven years.
Don't come Saturday. I'll find someone else. Someone who actually shows up.
She walked away. Four percent followed her down the hall like a little red ghost.
And it got worse. I'd made nineteen promises, and on Thursday, a lot of them came due at once.
One by one, the numbers started falling. Coach, thirty-five. Mr. Hale, sixty-eight. Mom, sixty-one.
I'd tried to buy trust with promises. But a promise isn't money. It's a loan. And I couldn't pay them back.
That night, every number on my list was lower than when I started.
I had made everything worse. With a superpower.
I went to the bathroom to wash my face. And when I looked up at the mirror, I stopped breathing.
There was a number above my own head. I'd never thought to check. Twenty-two percent.
Twenty-two. Lower than Jordan. Lower than a stranger. That was how much I trusted myself.
And it made sense. I'd broken promises to myself, too. Study tomorrow. Start running Monday. Call Maya back later.
Maybe that's why I made extra promises. I never believed I'd keep any.
You've been in there twenty minutes. Are you okay?
I almost said I'm fine. The automatic lie. Instead, I opened the door and told her everything except the numbers.
Maya. Jordan. Theo's milk. Nineteen promises. She listened to the whole thing sitting on the edge of the bathtub.
You can't fix eleven years in one week, sweetheart. Trust isn't a sprint. Nobody is grading you this Friday.
But you can keep one promise. Even one she told you to cancel. Especially that one.
Her number moved while she talked. Sixty-one. Sixty-three. The ugly truth was the only thing that never failed me.
Friday, I did something I'd never done. I went through my list and cancelled promises. Out loud. To people's faces.
I told Coach I couldn't come early every day. Just Tuesdays, for real. His number went up. Thirty-eight.
It sounds backwards. Cancelling a promise raised trust. But an honest no is worth more than a fake yes.
Then I found Theo in the library. Same green hoodie. Same thick book. Eighty percent.
I left you alone at lunch. There's no excuse. I wanted the cool table more than I wanted to keep my word.
Yeah. That one stung. But you came here and said it. Most people just pretend it never happened.
Eighty-one. Small. But it moved.
For the record, Jordan doesn't keep secrets. He collects them, like trading cards. You just handed him a rare one.
That explained Jordan. It didn't excuse me. She told me, and I passed it on.
Theo, will you sit with me at lunch on Monday? I'm asking, not promising. I'll prove it on Monday.
Bring your own milk.
Saturday. Five thirty in the morning. It was pouring rain. And Maya had told me not to come.
I came anyway. First bus, then second bus. I was outside her building at six forty-five. Soaked.
I didn't text. I didn't knock. If she came out alone, I'd carry the canvases. If she came with someone else, I'd go home.
At eight twenty, the door opened. Maya was holding three huge canvases wrapped in plastic, struggling with every one.
Nobody else had come.
What are you doing here? I told you not to come.
I know. You don't have to talk to me. Just let me carry them. Then I'll go home.
Her number didn't move. Four percent. She looked at me for a long time. Then she handed me the biggest canvas.
Two buses. Forty minutes. We didn't talk. I held the plastic over the canvases like a roof, so the rain wouldn't touch them.
On the second bus, I looked up. Four. Five. Seven. Barely anything. But for the first time in years, it went up.
At the academy, a lady at the desk said portfolios closed at nine sharp. It was eight fifty-two.
Maya ran. I ran behind her with three dripping canvases. At eight fifty-eight, she slid them across the desk.
We made it.
She said we. Not I. I noticed that. I think she did too.
On the way out, she stopped under the awning. Why did you come? Really?
Because you said nobody shows up for you. And I've been the main nobody for eleven years. I wanted to stop.
She was quiet. Then she said something I didn't expect.
Jordan texted me last night. He said sorry. He said he'd already guessed, and you begged him not to tell. He spread it anyway.
So Jordan, the guy with twenty-eight percent, did one honest thing. Even he could move a number.
I still should have asked you first. Before I believed it.
No. You had eleven years of reasons. I gave you every single one.
Her number jumped. Not a lot. Twelve. Fifteen. Eighteen. It would take a long time to fill that jar again.
Next Saturday. My grandma's piano. Still not moved. Interested?
I'll be there. Then I fixed it. Actually, I'm not promising. I'm just going to be there.
She laughed. It was the best sound I'd heard all week.
Monday, I sat with Theo. I brought my own milk. Jordan waved from the other table. I waved back, and stayed where I was.
Theo's number went up to eighty-four. He pretended not to notice that I noticed.
I passed the retake with a seventy-eight. Not amazing. But I told Mom the real score before she even asked.
Over the next month, I kept things small. Fewer promises. Every one of them kept.
Coach, forty-eight. Mr. Hale, seventy-nine. Maya, thirty-six. Then forty-one. Then, after the piano, fifty.
Yes, we moved the piano. Yes, it was heavier than a car. No, I'm never doing it again. I promised myself that one.
Then one morning, I woke up and the numbers were gone. Mom made toast, and her head was just a head.
I panicked for a second. Then I realized I didn't need them anymore. I could feel trust now, without seeing it.
It's in the way Maya hands me the biggest box without asking. The way Theo saves me a seat. The way Mom doesn't double-check.
The last number I ever saw was in the mirror, the night before they disappeared. Above my own head. Sixty-one percent.
Not perfect. But I'd started believing my own words again.
Here's what I learned. Trust isn't one big moment. It's a thousand tiny ones that nobody sees.
Every I'll be there. Every I won't tell. Every honest no. They all count. Even when you can't see the number.
So next time you make a promise, small or big, imagine a number floating above that person's head. Then keep it.
Oh, and Maya got into the academy. She leaves in the fall. And I already know who's carrying the canvases.
